places.notes: [Ramen · the 24-hour bowl under Dotonbori's giant dragon] Minami's famous all-night ramen stand, known for the huge dragon sculpture over the shop. There are only two choices, ramen (¥900 in October 2026, after a ¥200 rise) or chashu ramen, in a tonkotsu the listing describes as rich, made from pork bones and chicken feet with a secret tare. Most 2026 diners found it surprisingly light, with medium-thin, slightly curly noodles. The fun is the free kimchi, garlic and garlic chives to load in. Take a number and carry your bowl from the counter to tatami or counter seats. Queues are mostly overseas visitors late at night but move fast. Opinions vary: a nostalgic finish to a night out for many, lukewarm and thin for one critic.

places.notes: [Ramen · Kamukura's light cabbage ramen on its home street] The Dotonbori shop of Kamukura, now a nationwide chain that long-time fans still call a local treasure, with 71 seats and open from 10:00 to 08:00 the next morning. The signature "delicious ramen" (¥850 in October 2026) is a light, gently sweet, secret-recipe broth heaped with crunchy napa cabbage and thin-sliced pork. The most popular version adds small chashu and a soft-boiled egg (¥1,270); there's kara-age (¥430), gyoza and seasonal bowls such as a hot-and-sour soup with Zhenjiang vinegar and cilantro. Order on the table tablet. It's easy to eat and veg-heavy, though one diner found it too salty, and the noodles are soft, almost udon-like.

places.notes: [Ramen · Osaka Black, the jet-black shoyu, through the night] Since 2011 the Dotonbori branch of Kinkuemon, a shop famous for sharp shoyu ramen, set just off the main strip by the Kinryū queue. It has 41 seats over two floors and is open through the night (24 hours Friday to Sunday). The signature Osaka Black is a glossy jet-black soy broth with chicken stock and a seafood edge, buttery chicken-fat aroma and a faintly bitter soy finish. Choose thin noodles (most recommend them) or thick, topped with chashu, menma, green onion and a soft egg; extra noodles are extra. Also on the menu: Red Shoyu, King Shoyu, and Osaka Kinjou Shoyu, a clear chicken-and-light-soy broth that one 34-visit regular likes at 8 am. Buy a ticket at the machine outside; garlic on request. ¥1,000–1,200 a bowl; a few found it pricey for tourists or the service curt.

places.notes: [Ramen · Tokyo's Hayashida right under the Glico sign] The first Kansai branch, opened in 2022, of Ramen Hayashida, a Shinjuku shop famous for queues and run by INGS Co. It's a 16-seat counter one floor below the Glico running man, southwest of Ebisubashi. The signature is a clear shoyu broth of duck and Daisen-dori chicken (¥900; the special with a "Maximum Koitama" egg ¥1,200) on firm, thin whole-wheat noodles, with pork-shoulder and chicken-breast chashu. There's also a creamy chicken paitan, a refined tsukemen (special ¥1,250), mazesoba with truffle-sauce egg, and summer yuzu cold ramen (¥950) with yuzu jelly. Add a TKG or oyakodon (¥350–400). Buy tickets at the entrance machine. Light and quick, with friendly staff: a handy fast lunch when Minami's big names are queuing.

places.notes: [Ramen · Himeji back-fat tonkotsu, round the clock] The Dotonbori branch, opened 31 October 2025, of Zundōya, a Himeji-founded chain with over a hundred shops (about 106 in Japan and 4 in Shanghai, per a December 2025 visitor). It sits just east of Ebisubashi and is open 24 hours. The broth is pork bone with a slightly creamy soy seasoning and as much back fat as you choose (light, regular, rich or extra rich). Noodles are house-made: ultra-thin straight (recommended) or curly. The motomi (original) ramen is ¥860, ajitama ¥980, and all-toppings up to ¥1,360; summer brought a cold ramen with grated daikon. Season at the table with pepper, pickled ginger, garlic, chili oil, sesame and takana. Buy a ticket outside (transit IC accepted) and head upstairs. A Kansai-friendly tonkotsu with a hint of sweetness.

chef_bio.background: Chain founded in Himeji (zundouya.com).

Fans call it Osaka soul food from before the chain went national: a light, slightly sweet, almost Western-style broth loaded with napa cabbage, the kind people want after drinking instead of heavy tonkotsu. Buy a ticket at the machine out front. Service can be flat late at night, and one summer visitor found the cabbage bitter.

places.notes: [Ramen · beef-bone white soup, all night] An 18-seat counter, since 2011, three doors east of Mitsudera, serving Makotoya's beef-bone "gyū-paitan" around the clock. Regulars go when they want something that isn't miso, shoyu or shio. The beef broth is rich and smooth but not heavy, with a beefy aroma and sweetness that clings to thin noodles (choose your firmness). The favourite is the spicy red version with soft-boiled egg, chashu, wood ear, bean sprouts and green onion in a red bowl. Doctor it at the table with fresh garlic, garlic chips, pickled ginger and white sesame. Morioka cold noodles were ¥1,010 in August 2026. Buy a ticket at the machine by the door; one visitor found the street queue was for the malatang shop nearby.

places.gf_detail: The restaurant tells FindMeGlutenFree that every food item can be made gluten-free on request, but asks for notice when you book: "Advance reservation required for gluten-free dining." It makes its own gluten-free sauces, including soy sauce and ponzu. Celiac reviewers on FMGF (14 recent ratings) describe staff who confirm gluten-free at the table, swap single items in a set and change the grill between gluten-free and regular dishes. One 2025 diner was brought regular sauces by a different server and caught it by asking. It is not a gluten-free kitchen. Say you are celiac when you book and again when you sit down.
places.vegan_detail: A Matsusaka-beef yakiniku house. Replying on FMGF, the manager says it also offers vegan menu options, but no vegan dish is described anywhere. Ask when booking.

places.notes: [Yakiniku · gluten-free Matsusaka beef by Hōzenji] The "hanare" annex of Yakiniku M's Hōzenji branch: a second-floor room off Hōzenji Yokochō where you take your shoes off at the door, with seven tables, six of them semi-private and one a private room. Matsusaka beef is grilled at the table. It is a celiac favourite: the restaurant says any dish can be made gluten-free with notice, and it makes its own gluten-free soy sauce, ponzu and dipping sauces, so the marinated beef and garlic rice can be done too. Celiac reviewers rave about the staff ("Best GF meal we've had in Japan"). It is pricey: one diner put it at ¥8,800–12,000 a head, another had the ¥12,000 premium course. When it was full, staff walked guests to another branch nearby. Book and mention gluten-free when you do.

chef_bio.background: Part of the Matsusakagyu Yakiniku M group of Osaka yakiniku restaurants (official site); one FMGF reviewer counted four locations.

places.name: 源氏蕎麦 法善寺参道店 (Genji Soba)
places.gf_detail: The soba is hand-made from 100% buckwheat (juwari). The menu marks gluten-free dishes, and celiac reviewers on FindMeGlutenFree (101 recent ratings) describe a separate, celiac-labelled section. On the official menu, the tempura is made with buckwheat and rice flour and "Fried in a Dedicated Gluten-Free Fryer". Gluten-free dipping sauce and soy sauce are made for gluten-free orders, while the regular sauces are also in use, so ask. FMGF flags that it is NOT a dedicated gluten-free facility. Several reviewers say the celiac-safe tempura and menu are dinner only. Staff ask whether you are celiac. Tell them, and reserve the set courses ahead.
places.vegan_detail: The set courses note: "Gluten-Free & Vegan options are available upon advance request." There is a vegan soba on the à la carte menu, but in September 2026 a reviewer was asked whether egg was OK after ordering it, so it may only be vegetarian. Ask about the dashi and egg.
places.hours_raw: 11:30–21:30 (L.O. 21:30), break 14:30–17:00; closed some Wednesdays (水曜不定休) (official site). Lunch and dinner set courses by reservation, upstairs. Reviewers say the celiac-safe tempura is dinner only. The original shop at Namba 4-5-8 is closed for now; this Hōzenji Sandō shop opened in March 2026.

places.cuisine: 100% buckwheat soba, hand-cut in the window · cold zaru and hot soba · prawn and vegetable tempura from a dedicated GF fryer · beef and duck soba · lunch and dinner set courses (¥3,300 / ¥4,800) · since 1929
places.notes: [Soba · 100% buckwheat and gluten-free tempura on Hōzenji Sandō] A soba house founded in 1929 that moved in March 2026 into a new shop on the stone-paved Hōzenji approach; the old shop is closed for now. The noodles are hand-made from 100% buckwheat (you can watch them being cut in the front window), which makes it a celiac favourite. The menu marks gluten-free and celiac-safe dishes, and the prawn and vegetable tempura is made with buckwheat and rice flour in a dedicated gluten-free fryer. The classic order is cold zaru soba with a big wild prawn and vegetable tempura (¥2,950). There are also grated-daikon, yam and Tamba black-bean natto soba, beef and duck soba, a two-soba lunch (¥1,850), and set courses upstairs by reservation. Some find the broth fishy. You order by QR code at the table, and dinner waits can stretch at busy times.

chef_bio.background: Genji Soba ran at Namba 4-5-8; in March 2026 it opened on Hōzenji Sandō, and the new-shop letter is signed 「源氏蕎麦法善寺参道本店 鳥倉 荘一」. The site describes soba-making demonstrations in Melbourne (2023) and Canberra (2024–2026) and soba sold through Takashimaya and other department stores.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「変わらぬ手打ちと、蕎麦本来の味を大切に、日本の文化を食べるお店として」 (new-shop letter, March 2026).

places.notes: [Sweets · vegan and gluten-free tarts off Dotonbori] A tiny, quiet cake shop on a Namba side street with about four seats. Everything is vegan and gluten-free, and it is a celiac favourite (FMGF marks it reported dedicated gluten-free). Expect small tarts and cakes, around ¥1,000 each: mango, mixed berry cheesecake, chocolate pistachio, matcha and white chocolate, strawberry chocolate. Reviewers single out the cashew cream on a coarse almond crust, and the rice-flour and coconut-oil cookies, which one family bought to take home after being given some free. There is Italian espresso and peach cream soda. Service is gentle, once by a host in a kimono, though one 2026 diner found it unfriendly. Takeaway, and an online shop.

places.name: Gluten-Free Vegan OKONOMIYAKI Vim
places.gf_detail: A gluten-free okonomiyaki restaurant. FindMeGlutenFree marks it "Reported to be dedicated gluten-free", and celiac reviewers (through October 2026) call it entirely gluten-free and safe for coeliacs, with Kirin gluten-free and organic gluten-free beer. Reported features include a dedicated gluten-free fryer and kitchen. The restaurant itself publishes nothing beyond its name, so this rests on community reports. Confirm when you book.
places.vegan_detail: Despite "Vegan" in its name, the menu also has meat and seafood: reviewers ate pork-belly okonomiyaki, grilled scallops, fried chicken and pork noodles. The vegan options include battered tofu and rice balls ("some vegan options"). Ask whether the batter, sauce and dashi for the vegan dishes are plant-based.
places.hours_raw: No hours published. Reviewers: opens at 17:00 (June 2026); closed Thursdays (April 2026); once closed an hour early (October 2026). About six seats. Reservation strongly advised (booking online needs a Japanese phone number); queue before opening otherwise. No children under 18 (FMGF tip, June 2026). One meal and one drink per person (May 2026).

places.cuisine: Gluten-free okonomiyaki (pork belly and vegan) · stir-fried noodles and pasta · oyster mushrooms · battered tofu · grilled scallops · fried chicken · Kirin gluten-free beer · six seats
places.notes: [Okonomiyaki · gluten-free okonomiyaki off Dotonbori] A tiny gluten-free okonomiyaki spot up a narrow alley off Dotonbori, with a counter downstairs and one table upstairs (about six seats). For celiac travellers it is a rare safe way to eat Osaka's signature dish. Reviewers order pork-belly okonomiyaki, stir-fried noodles and pasta, oyster mushrooms, tempura, battered tofu with rice balls, grilled scallops and fried chicken, with a Kirin gluten-free beer. The name says vegan, but meat and seafood are on the menu, so ask. Book ahead (online booking needs a Japanese phone number) or queue before the 5 pm opening. Several were turned away. Portions are small and prices high, one meal and one drink per person is expected, under-18s are not admitted, and it is reported closed on Thursdays. One reviewer mentions a sister restaurant around the corner.

chef_bio.background: A gluten-free okonomiyaki restaurant; the official page (nanbavim.biz-option.com) gives only its name, phone and links. One reviewer names the host-chef as Miyo.

anecdotes.text: "Tiny restaurant with a counter downstairs and a single table upstairs… oyster mushrooms, stir fried pasta, and of course the okonomiyaki." — FMGF review, October 2026.

places.notes: [Ramen · the Shōwa-style chuka soba with the long queue] The Namba shop of Fujii, a small chain selling "nostalgic Shōwa flavour" chuka soba from Tokyo to Osaka. A sharp, easy-drinking shoyu broth comes with back fat you can scale down, and one diner was reminded of Onomichi ramen. Watch the fried rice being made at the counter: fluffy, and one regular's favourite anywhere. The ramen, kara-age and fried rice set is a generous ¥1,100 (October 2026). Nira soba piled with garlic chives arrived on 1 July 2026, served with a perforated ladle to catch them. Add garlic powder or vinegar halfway. Queues are the catch: 40 minutes to an hour and a half in October 2026, once 45 groups ahead on a Saturday. Take a number at the shop and wander until your phone pings. Closed Tuesdays; open to 3 am on Fridays and Saturdays.

It is usually run by one person, so expect to wait while earlier orders go out. Two lines: a tonkotsu with one big slab of tender chashu, looking thick but drinking easily, and a back-fat shoyu with black pepper that is lighter than it looks. The umami miso tonkotsu (¥1,550 in May 2026) gets an accent from marinated onions, and the back-fat shoyu was ¥1,350. Add a tsukimi chashu rice bowl (¥500). The thin noodles run soft, which may divide people, and one diner tasted oden in the broth. It's cashless (card or PayPay), the only drinks are alcohol, and there's no restroom nearby. Often quiet, with no queue (September 2026).

places.notes: [Ramen · Minami's 24-hour pork-bone shoyu with free kimchi] A 17-seat, mostly counter shop on the shopping street by Hōzenji, open 24 hours and run by Arakawa Food Service. For years it was a late-night ritual for locals (one did "the sauna at Amza, then Hanamaruken"). The base is a pork-bone soy broth, rich but not heavy, with medium-thin noodles. The signature torokotsu ramen comes with two big pieces of tender pork, nori, menma, naruto and green onion. Free kimchi on the counter cuts the richness. Newer additions include garlic tonkotsu ramen (April 2026) and champon, and the fried rice has a following. Regulars say the old queues have eased, the crowd is now largely overseas visitors, and the regular bowl tastes lighter than before. The restroom is up narrow stairs.

places.notes: [Ramen · beef-bone white soup on Sennichimae] A ramen shop since 2023 on the Sennichimae side of Hōzenji, full of overseas visitors even on weekdays. The draw is a frothy beef-bone and chicken white soup: rich and creamy but easy to finish, built on chicken carcass and beef knuckle with a soy kaeshi and back-fat finish over thin straight noodles. It comes with two chashu, one charred and one tender, plus a runny seasoned egg, menma and green onion. There's also a lighter tonkotsu and a mala-style chili condiment on the table. Prices are high: a limited bowl topped ¥2,000 in September 2026, and the strip-loin rice bowl in the set ran salty. One diner flagged cleanliness. Cards and electronic payment accepted.

It is larger than its sisters: 14 tables, seven of them in private rooms, curtained semi-private seating, a hall for groups of up to 32, a lift, and wheelchair access to the table. Matsusaka-beef courses are grilled at the table. For celiac diners the draw is the sauces, which the general manager says are all gluten-free. Staff even bring out the labelled soy sauce bottle, and one server who is celiac comes up again and again in reviews. Reviewers had non-GF set-course items swapped, though one notes the soup is the exception. Dinner daily, plus weekend lunch.

places.notes: [Ramen · offal ramen in a bubbling clay pot, round the clock] A small, 24-hour Sennichimae-arcade branch of Horumon Ramen 8910, whose main shop is in Shimoshinjo, Higashiyodogawa. The bowl arrives bubbling in a clay pot that keeps it hot to the end, loaded with tender, fluffy horumon in a hearty broth with no off-odour. Choose red (spicy, the popular one) or white. One diner liked it topped with corn. The shop nudges you to finish with rice in the broth, risotto- or porridge-style. A salt-seasoned kalbi rice bowl is the alternative. It's like a one-person hot pot, good after drinks or, as one inspector found, for an early breakfast. Rarely crowded. Cash only.

places.notes: [Ramen · Miyazaki karamen round the clock in Sōemonchō] A 24-hour, two-floor, 23-seat karamen shop in the Sōemonchō nightlife streets, since 2011. The signature karakara noodles arrive bright red under fluffy scrambled egg, garlic chives and minced meat, with real umami behind the heat and the egg adding creaminess. Pick your spice level, up to 100 (regulars brag about levels 30, 50 and 100), and your noodles, including konjac. Add tender pork if you like. For milder tastes there's a Hokkaido "100-year" miso ramen, and a cult omurice that one 2 am regular orders instead of noodles. It is kept cool inside, anticipating the heat. A post-drinks staple. The street outside can feel rough late at night.
